title: Hazel and the Portrait
premise: Folklorist Coral Marchetti returns to her grandmother's house in the village of Hazel's Hollow to archive songs no one will sing twice. She discovers that every photograph taken in the house now contains an extra empty chair—and when she sits to record the last surviving singer, she is pulled into the chair, into a liminal parlor where the missing villagers of 1974 wait. The village survived that winter by giving up seven people and burning their portraits; Coral must return what was taken—her grandmother's stolen memory of naming them—to free them before the house finishes claiming her as its eighth resident.
about_author: Marguerite Voss is the pen name of an archivist who spent a decade cataloguing oral histories in remote mountain villages, where she learned that some recordings should never be played back. She writes horror about what families agree not to remember.

chapters.title: The Chair That Wasn't There
chapters.summary: Coral arrives at her late grandmother's house to catalogue its contents, documenting everything as ritual against grief. Comparing old family photographs with fresh scans, she finds an extra wooden chair appearing in images across decades—always empty, always closer to center frame. POV: Coral. Emotional beat: unease disguised as professional curiosity; the reader feels documentation becoming compulsion.

chapters.title: What the Village Won't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Coral interviews elderly residents about a 1974 flood song; each refuses after one verse, and one woman begs her to delete the recording. In the house that night, the tape plays verses no one sang, and Coral wakes inside the photograph's parlor, facing seven gaunt figures and the chair now holding her shape. POV: Coral. Emotional beat: dread crystallizing into entrapment.

chapters.title: Seven Names, One Winter
chapters.summary: Inside the parlor, time pools like standing water. The seven reveal the bargain: the village fed them to the house to survive the flood year, then burned their portraits so they couldn't be mourned. Only Coral's grandmother, the youngest survivor, was made to forget their names—the payment that sealed it. Coral realizes returning the names means shattering her family's founding story. POV: Coral. Emotional beat: rising desperation and moral vertigo.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Coral bargains her way out with the last unburned portrait fragment: her own face, half-formed. Back in the house, she sings all seven names into the recorder and plays it aloud until the walls listen, restoring the village's stolen memory at the cost of her grandmother's peaceful lies. The chair vanishes from every photograph except one—empty again, waiting politely. POV: Coral. Emotional beat: catharsis shadowed by survival's permanent cost.
